extracted.intended_audience: stand-up comedians (from open-mic newcomers to seasoned pros) seeking to get booked
extracted.subtask_short: getting booked as a stand-up comedian
extracted.subtask_description: Practical advice on preparing submission materials (video, bio, availabilities) and on networking/contact behavior to increase chances of being booked for shows and festivals.

rubrics_metrics.name: A recent, high quality video clip
rubrics_metrics.description: Your video clip should be uploaded to YouTube or Vimeo, so you can send a link and make it easy for the booker to see your set. It doesn’t have to be professionally recorded and edited (although that is always nice!).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make sure the clip is recent and is a good representation of your act. Check audio quality, focus and camera stability — clips with bad audio, out of focus, shaky camera, etc. make it difficult to see your talent. Don’t use a bad clip just because it’s from an established club or prominent festival. Pro-tip: double- and triple-check that the link you send can be viewed ("This video is private" is a great way to not get a booking). Film as many of your sets as possible so you have options; you never know when you’ll deliver the perfect set (or the biggest dud). The site references a short video on how NOT to film a clip as useful guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Your bio
rubrics_metrics.description: Your bio should be short, sweet and to the point about how great you are and all the prominent shows or festivals you’ve done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be truthful. Indicate whether you have a clean set or are more geared towards adults, whether your jokes are story based or one-liners, and why you’re unique. Don’t make your bio a poorly written joke. For festivals, include credits for regular gigs, other festivals you’ve performed in or famous comics you’ve worked with.

rubrics_metrics.name: How much time you can do
rubrics_metrics.description: Do you have 5, 10, 15 or 45 minutes? Make sure you know how much quality stage time you can do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is not total raw material you’ve ever written — it means how much solid, polished material you can provide that gets laughs reliably. Never lie about how much time you can do: if you claim a tight 20 minutes but only have a strong 5, you won’t get booked again.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include your tools in outreach (video, bio, avails)
rubrics_metrics.description: A general form letter makes it easier to send out your available dates or "avails" to various venues and bookers; it should include all 3 of your Tools of the Trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare a concise outreach message that attaches/links your video, includes your short bio, and lists how much time you can do and available dates — this streamlines the booker’s decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the booker’s preferred contact method
rubrics_metrics.description: When contacting a booker be sure to use their preferred contact method. Sometimes it’s through an individual or individuals, sometimes it’s through a Facebook group page, other times it’s an email or a website form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify correct contact information before reaching out. Bookers get many requests; contacting them through the wrong channel (e.g., social media when they prefer email) might mean you won’t be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be professional and courteous (never demand a spot)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether it’s a stranger, an acquaintance or good bud, always be professional and courteous. Never demand to be put on a show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a friend runs a show, the same rules apply: be proactive and polite inquiring about a slot rather than expecting or demanding placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t ask for a specific showcase slot from multi-event producers
rubrics_metrics.description: When contacting a booker or club owner who produces multiple events, try not to ask for a specific showcase slot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you request a particular slot and you’re not the right fit for that specific showcase, you may not get booked at all. Be open to other opportunities the producer might have.

rubrics_metrics.name: Network actively with other comics and producers
rubrics_metrics.description: A big part of comedy is networking: going to mics & talking to comics you share lineups with is great, but take it further and go to shows you’re not on & introduce yourself to the people running it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seeing what producers put on and complimenting their work can form relationships; if they know you’re stopping by, you might score a guest set or a future booking. Regular attendance, polite introductions, and relationship-building can yield opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make festival submissions count (use best clip & bio; include credits)
rubrics_metrics.description: When it comes to festivals, use those tools in your kit and show them how great you are! Festivals are incredibly competitive and the bigger the fest, the more applications they receive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put your best foot forward: submit your best-quality clip (clearly seen and heard), a well-written truthful bio with credits, and accurately represent your time/availability. A bad video or a bio that’s just a poorly written joke can keep you off the lineup. Note festivals can receive hundreds of submissions and some charge fees — treat the application seriously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain persistence, humility, and professionalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t get down on yourself if you’re not getting booked — the more you believe in what you do, the more people will take notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Success favors those who are persistent, humble and talented. Perseverance is rewarded: keep working, communicating, acting professional and keep at it. The article explicitly says: 'If you work hard, communicate, act professional and keep at it, you WILL get booked!'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize quality of material over claiming long sets
rubrics_metrics.description: This does NOT mean taking every idea or unpolished bit you ever came up with to tell a booker you can go 45 minutes. It means how much solid material can you provide on stage, which of those bits have been worked on over and over, and what gets a laugh every time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It may take months or years to develop a quality 5–10 minutes suitable for audiences. Present only the amount of stage time you can consistently deliver well; overpromising harms repeat booking chances.
